source: Wolff & Barbey (2015) Causal reasoning with forces
finding: Force theory composes causal relations by adding force vectors. In animations of car chains, modal answers matched its predictions in nearly all chains (Exp 1a, 1b).
numbers: Exp 1a N=24, 18 animations; Exp 1b N=25, 9 chains. Only miss: first relation of the CAUSE/ALLOW chain, chi2(3,N=24)=3.25, p=.355 (chance). Other chains e.g. ALLOW/ALLOW chi2(3,N=25)=21.56, p<.0001.
limits: Small samples, 1-D car collisions, Emory undergraduates. The authors built the animations to fit the theory.
agent_relevance: Chaining causal links is predictable from a small rule set, so a scaffold could compute chain outcomes from a table instead of asking the model.

source: Wolff & Barbey (2015) Causal reasoning with forces
finding: Double prevention (prevent then prevent) is the discriminating case. Force and causal-model theories predict ALLOW or CAUSE; mental-model theory predicts PREVENT. Animations and real-world chains gave ALLOW/CAUSE, but typed answers on vague psychological terms gave PREVENT.
numbers: Whole-chain P/P split 50% CAUSE / 50% ALLOW in Exp 1a and 1b. Exp 3 modal P/P answer ALLOW 39%. Exp 2 (N=20) PREVENT 65%. Force theory predicted ALLOW 62%, CAUSE 38%.
limits: The authors blame an 'atmosphere' effect for Exp 2; this is a post-hoc account. The same chain gets different answers by format.
agent_relevance: Double prevention is an ambiguity trap. An agent should list both readings (cause, allow) and not commit to one wording.

source: Wolff & Barbey (2015) Causal reasoning with forces
finding: Exp 2 re-ran the 16 chains of Goldvarg & Johnson-Laird (2001, Exp 4) with psychological terms. Force and causal-model theories scored 14/16, mental-model theory 13/16.
numbers: N=20 typed conclusions. Force/causal 14/16 (binomial p<.01); mental model 13/16 (p<.05). Force and causal both missed P/P (observed PREVENT 65%) and not-C/A (observed not-CAUSE 50%). Mental model missed A/P, A/not-C, not-C/A. People gave PREVENT 80% for A/P and 70% for A/not-C, where G&JL found ALLOW-not.
limits: Only 20 people; the authors coded free responses themselves. Not an independent lab replication.
agent_relevance: Where theories differ by one item the data are thin. Do not build hard rules on single chain types.

source: Wolff & Barbey (2015) Causal reasoning with forces
finding: On 192 real-world causal chains (32 compositions), force and causal-model theories beat mental-model theory.
numbers: Exp 3 N=40, 96 chains each, 10 response options. Force and causal model 30/32 correct (p<.000001); mental model 26/32 (p<.001). Friedman chi2(2)=8.00, p=.018. Both missed not-C-not/A and not-C-not/P.
limits: The gap is 4 compositions. The misses rest on a 'matching assumption' the authors say may need relaxing.
agent_relevance: Real text chains are mostly handled by simple composition rules. Supports a small rule table for chain steps.

source: Wolff & Barbey (2015) Causal reasoning with forces
finding: With three-link chains force and causal-model theories hold; mental-model theory falls to chance.
numbers: Exp 4 N=24, 25 chains. Force 23/25 correct, causal model 23/25, mental model 14/25 (p=0.69 vs chance). Friedman chi2(2)=18.00, p<.001. If causal-model credit needs an unambiguous prediction it scores 18/25 vs force 23/25. Example: C/C/C modal answer CAUSE 77%; A/C/C observed ALLOW 54%, CAUSE 38% (predicted 62%, 38%).
limits: Causal-model score depends on how ties are counted. Result tables were only partly read.
agent_relevance: Longer chains stay predictable by composition rules; the LLM need not reason them freely.

source: Wolff & Barbey (2015) Causal reasoning with forces
finding: Force theory says CAUSE-then-PREVENT always gives PREVENT, but PREVENT-then-CAUSE gives PREVENT only 37% of the time. The same chain can give different valid answers.
numbers: Predicted PREVENT 100% (C then P) vs 37% (P then C). Authors say double preventions are 'potentially ambiguous between CAUSE and ALLOW'.
limits: Force magnitudes are not specified, so predictions are probabilistic and need simulation.
agent_relevance: Order of links changes the result; an agent must keep order explicit when composing.

source: Khemlani, Bello, Briggs, Harner, Nazari, Johnson-Laird (2020) Much ado about nothing: the mental representation of omissive relations
finding: Experiments 1 and 2 contradict a force-theory prediction: people infer time order from omissive causes (not-A caused B) just as for ordinary causes. Force vectors carry no time.
numbers: Exp 1 N=50 (MTurk): 'yes' to cause-before-effect 64% vs effect-before-cause 8%, B=3.85, p<.0001; omissive vs orthodox 35% vs 37%, p=.22. Exp 2 N=50: 'before' when cause first 78% vs 12%; 'after' 79% vs 12%; omissive vs orthodox 'before' 43% vs 47%, Wilcoxon p=.09, Cliff's delta=.11.
limits: Fictional magic-spell materials, MTurk. Force-theory authors could answer that time order enters from other knowledge.
agent_relevance: A scaffold using force dynamics needs a separate time field; force vectors alone do not order events.

source: Khemlani, Bello, Briggs, Harner, Nazari, Johnson-Laird (2020) Much ado about nothing: the mental representation of omissive relations
finding: Experiment 3: people list 'privileged' possibilities first and fastest for omissive causes, as model theory says; this also counts against a counterfactual-contrast account.
numbers: Omissive CAUSE: first-listed not-A&B 48%, A&B 26%, A&not-B 26%; orthodox CAUSE: A&B first 100%. Mean time to list A&B 10.24 s orthodox vs 15.68 s omissive. People listed 1 possibility on 26% of trials, 2 on 35%, 3 on 31%, all 4 on 8%. (Exp 3 N not read.)
limits: Listing tasks differ from judging animations. Authors back their own mental-model theory.
agent_relevance: Omission reasoning needs explicit lists of what happens and what does not. Fits an operator that enumerates cases.

source: Khemlani, Bello, Briggs, Harner, Nazari, Johnson-Laird (2020) Much ado about nothing: the mental representation of omissive relations
finding: The paper reports that 66% of people drew an omissive conclusion from 'not X causes Y; Y causes Z' (Briggs & Khemlani 2019) and says this replicates Wolff & Barbey (2015).
numbers: 66% spontaneously concluded 'not X causes Z'. Taken from the paper's introduction, not re-run.
limits: Second-hand summary of other studies.
agent_relevance: People compose omissive chains routinely; a model that drops the negation makes a human-unlike error.

source: Khemlani, Barbey & Johnson-Laird (2014) Causal reasoning with mental models
finding: Rival model theory: cause means 'given A, B occurs'; enable means 'given A, B is possible'. The authors say probabilistic accounts cannot separate cause from enable, and that force theory adds forces to model theory instead of replacing it.
numbers: Review. Listing tasks (Goldvarg & Johnson-Laird 2001): people list 3 possibilities for 'cause' (2 for the strong reading) and 4 for weak 'enable'; enabling is more confusing than causing.
limits: Authors are the rival camp. No new numbers.
agent_relevance: The cause/enable split can be coded as a possibility table; a good LLM test is whether it lists the same table.

source: Khemlani, Barbey & Johnson-Laird (2014) Causal reasoning with mental models
finding: Neuroscience claim: lateral prefrontal cortex supports causal inference; Satpute et al. found dorsolateral PFC activity for causal vs associative relations. Courts in some places make no cause/enable distinction, yet people judge those who cause harm as more culpable than those who enable it (Frosch et al. 2007).
numbers: Review of fMRI; no new counts.
limits: The link to model theory over force theory is interpretive; both theories can claim it.
agent_relevance: Cause vs enable matters for blame wording. An agent writing about fault should keep the distinction.

source: Wolff & Song (2003) Models of causation and the semantics of causal verbs
finding: Five experiments with verb sorting and rating: the force-dynamic model fit the meaning of causal verbs better than focal-set models, which put CAUSE closer to ENABLE and PREVENT than those two are to each other.
numbers: Abstract only (Europe PMC record): five experiments; no N or effect sizes read.
limits: Not opened in full; sorting tasks on verbs, not behaviour.
agent_relevance: CAUSE, ENABLE, PREVENT are three roughly equidistant concepts, not one concept with two weaker cousins.

source: Wolff (2007) Representing causation
finding: Six experiments with physics-simulated 3-D animations: causal judgments use several forces, people combine forces with a qualitative rule, and the model extends to social causation.
numbers: Abstract only: Exp 1-3 several forces; Exp 4 qualitative resultant rule; Exp 5-6 social causation. No N read.
limits: Abstract only. Animations built from the authors' own vectors.
agent_relevance: Founding test of the vector model; numbers need pulling from the paper before use.

source: Sloman, Barbey & Hotaling (2009) A causal model theory of the meaning of cause, enable, and prevent
finding: Rival: cause, enable, prevent are links in a causal graph. Enable needs an alternative cause and A as a necessary category; prevent reduces likelihood. Accounts for four experiments.
numbers: Abstract only: four experiments, no counts read. In Wolff & Barbey Exp 4 it ties force theory at 23/25.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Easier to run as code than vector physics; the two could be pitted on the agent's own tasks.

source: Wolff, Barbey & Hausknecht (2010) For want of a nail: How absences cause events
finding: Force theory says an absence is causal when it removes a force. Supported by 3 animation experiments with force removal and 'virtual' forces, and a 4th on synonymy. Later challenged on time order by Khemlani et al. (2020).
numbers: Abstract only: 3 animation experiments plus a synonymy experiment.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Omission cases are a known weak point; test the agent there first.

source: Goksun, George, Hirsh-Pasek & Golinkoff (2013) Forces and motion: how young children understand causal events
finding: Preschoolers mostly grasp single and dual force interactions for cause, enable, prevent; only 5.5-year-olds integrate two contradictory forces.
numbers: Abstract: n=60, ages 3.5 to 5.5, board game predicting a ball's endpoint.
limits: Abstract only. Gardenfors (2021) adds that kids use a second force only when it points the same way.
agent_relevance: Same-direction forces are easiest, opposed forces hardest; present opposed forces step by step.

source: George, Goksun, Hirsh-Pasek & Golinkoff (2019) Any way the wind blows
finding: 5- and 6-year-olds could infer causes of single- and dual-force events, doing best when problems matched force arrays that language encodes (prevent = opposing forces).
numbers: Abstract: N=30.
limits: Abstract only; small N.
agent_relevance: Language-aligned structure helps inference.

source: Mayrhofer & Waldmann (2014) Indicators of causal agency in physical interactions
finding: Who counts as agent or patient in a launch depends on prior context (relative movement, visibility order, self-propulsion), not on the collision alone.
numbers: Abstract: two experiments with Michotte-style launching.
limits: Abstract only. A boundary for pure force models.
agent_relevance: Agent and patient roles can flip with context; agent prompts should state roles.

source: Ju & Kim (2024) Pushing the ball or pulling the rubber band (PsyArXiv preprint; published JEP:General 2026)
finding: Speed profile alone flips perceived force direction and material in an ambiguous stick/disc event. Acceleration before separation gives push and rigid; deceleration gives pull and elastic.
numbers: Exp 1 free report N=77 (40 accel, 37 decel): push 80.0% vs 12.5% in accel; pull 70.3% vs 16.2% in decel, chi2(1)=29, p<.001. Rigid 62.5% (accel) vs 5.4% (decel); elastic 25.0% vs 73.0%. Exp 2a/2b N=31/30. Causal vs material r=.96, CI [.88,.99]. Pre-separation speed chi2(4)=747.46, p<.001.
limits: Female undergraduates at one university; abstract shapes. Coders agreed 89.6% before consensus.
agent_relevance: Perceived force direction depends on cues outside the force vector. Text descriptions of events lose such cues.

source: Ju & Kim (2024) Pushing the ball or pulling the rubber band (PsyArXiv preprint; published JEP:General 2026)
finding: A pause-detection task shows the effect is perceptual, not only a verbal choice: sensitivity changed with the event category even when causal and material judgment were irrelevant.
numbers: Exp 3a d'=2.45 (decel) vs 1.60 (accel), t(29)=4.41, p<.001, d=0.80. Exp 3b 1.27 vs 2.11, t(29)=-5.33, d=-0.97. Exp 3c 2.25 vs 2.83, t(29)=-3.53, p=.001. 3b-3d reverse the 3a pattern once the rubber-band percept is removed.
limits: Preprint text read, not the journal version. N=30 per experiment.
agent_relevance: Force dynamics can be implicit in perception; LLMs have no such channel, only descriptions.

source: Cheung, Qiao, Brown & Lagnado (2026) Attribution of responsibility between agents in a causal chain
finding: When A orders B to harm V, people judge the executor (B) more causal and blameworthy than the instigator (A), even though A is more necessary.
numbers: Study 1 N=90: B causal M=58.4 vs A 41.6, d about 0.9-1.3. Study 2 N=256, Study 3 N=136, Study 4 N=384. Counterfactual likelihood of outcome without A 14.8% vs without B 22.6%.
limits: Force dynamics is only background; no force manipulation. UK Prolific vignettes. 37 of 136 failed the intent check in Study 3. Studies 1 and 3 not preregistered.
agent_relevance: Proximity to the harm pulls causal credit; an agent judging fault from text should not just follow the proximal actor.

source: Quillien, O'Neill & Henne (2025); Henne & O'Neill (2022); Thanawala & Erb (2024) on double prevention
finding: Double prevention is a live dispute. Thanawala & Erb argue order effects challenge causal pluralism and counterfactual theories; Quillien et al. show a counterfactual model reproduces those order effects; Henne & O'Neill find people call the first knocker causal and the second not.
numbers: Abstracts only. Henne & O'Neill: 4 experiments plus 3 supplemental. Thanawala & Erb: Exp 3-4, an unintentional double preventer can outrate an intentional affector when order changes.
limits: Abstracts only. Counterfactual models are a third rival to force theory on the same case.
agent_relevance: The double-prevention rule is not settled; do not use it as a hard check.

source: Gardenfors & Lombard (2018) Causal cognition, force dynamics and early hunting technologies
finding: Argues that variation in force dynamics (stabbing spear, throwing spear, atlatl, bow, poison) tracks grades of causal thinking in hominins.
numbers: Conceptual analysis: seven grades of causal thinking. No experiment.
limits: Interpretive archaeology; untested.
agent_relevance: Low direct use; shows force dynamics as a ladder from contact force to delayed forces.

source: Gardenfors (2021) Causal reasoning and event cognition as evolutionary determinants of language structure
finding: Summarises that adults combine forces (boat motor plus wind), and that 3-5 year olds fail with a second force unless it points the same way; says affector forces count as cause, enable or prevent depending on the counterforce.
numbers: Review of Goksun et al. (n=60) and Wolff. No new numbers.
limits: Review and evolutionary account, not an experiment.
agent_relevance: Same developmental order hint: opposed forces are harder.

source: Gardenfors (2025) The geometry and dynamics of meaning
finding: Generalises force dynamics to verb semantics: manner verbs need a force domain, result verbs need property-space vectors; the event model has agent force, counterforce and result vector.
numbers: Theory paper; resultant force = agent force plus counterforces.
limits: No empirical test. Related models: Talmy 1988, Wolff 2007, Croft 2012, Copley 2019.
agent_relevance: Gives a data layout (agent force, counterforce, result) that a scaffold could fill in.

source: Lynn (2026) Conceptual blending in humans and language models
finding: Claims language models carry only linguistic traces of image-schema and force-dynamic regularities (blockage, enablement, resistance) and lack goal-driven affordance use.
numbers: Conceptual analysis with a toy vector-symbolic Python demo; no benchmark scores.
limits: No measured LLM results; assertion only.
agent_relevance: A hypothesis, not a finding; no direct test of force dynamics in LLMs here.

source: Zadrozny (2025) Challenges and opportunities in causality analysis using LLMs
finding: Newer LLMs (GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Pro) agree highly on causal links between events in text; the paper notes annotation schemes mix many senses of 'cause' and that prevention clashes with counterfactual annotation rules.
numbers: Agreement 88-91% on causal relationships between events, vs typical human inter-annotator agreement 30-70%. BERT variants 85-91% F1 on a causal-extraction dataset, beating Llama and GPT-3.5 as of fall 2024.
limits: Agreement between models is not accuracy. No cause/enable/prevent split tested. Review plus small experiment.
agent_relevance: LLMs agreeing with each other does not show force-like structure; agreement is not a validity check.

source: Search gap, this run
finding: No LLM study that directly tests force-dynamic categories (cause, enable, prevent, resistance) was found with accessible tools; arXiv and Semantic Scholar were rate-limited and the web search budget was spent.
numbers: 0 direct LLM force-dynamics benchmarks found in Europe PMC; the 2020-2026 LLM items found (Lynn 2026, Zadrozny 2025) are conceptual or about general causal extraction.
limits: Failure to find is not evidence of absence; arXiv or ACL papers on causal-verb probing may exist.
agent_relevance: Treat 'LLMs handle force dynamics' as untested; run our own small test on cause/enable/prevent and double prevention.
